title: Europe launches €95m semi-autonomous ship in Estonia
content:
The Union’s newest naval vessel is to provide surveillance and to protect undersea infrastructure. The EUROGUARD is not yet in service; developers say testing is the point of the exercise.

Europe has launched a new kind of naval vessel. The EUROGUARD semi-autonomous ship went through its launch in Nasva, Estonia, on the Baltic Sea. The 45-metre craft is to strengthen maritime surveillance and help protect Europe’s coasts. The European Commission says it will support member states facing growing risks at sea.

Those risks are real, according to the Commission. Threats to undersea cables, energy infrastructure, and strategic maritime routes are rising. The purpose of the vessel is to help member states respond to them.

The EUROGUARD project began in 2022. It brings together 29 organisations from 10 European countries. The Estonian shipyard Baltic Workboats coordinates the work. The European Defence Fund has contributed €65m of a total budget of about €95m.

title: Outspend and outproduce Russia, Kubilius exhorts business summit
content:
Europeans are still too slow in paying the price of peace. The price of war would be higher, Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said on Wednesday.

Russia will spend about as much on its military next year as all EU member states combined, according to EU Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius. He made the claim at the European Business Summit in Brussels on 18 November 2026. For Mr Kubilius, the conclusion is stark. Europe is not yet deterring Moscow, and that must change.

The numbers are large. Russia plans to allocate €180bn to its military next year, a 33 per cent increase on this year. In purchasing power parity terms, that matches or slightly exceeds the €500–550bn that all member states will spend together. Mr Kubilius said Russia’s war economy remains able to expand production and to innovate.

Mr Kubilius said Russia was not being deterred. It was escalating attacks on Ukraine and waging a hybrid war against Europe. “We need first of all to outspend Russia in defence and to outproduce Russia in defence.” The question, he said, is whether the EU is doing enough at every level.
snippet: Europeans are still too slow in paying the price of peace. The price of war would be higher, Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said on Wednesday.
creator: Daniel Deyl

title: Mediterranean net is cast wide as Kallas’s absence raises eyebrows
content:
Security arrangements between the EU and its regional southern partners must address everybody’s concerns, the EU-MED Security Forum 2026 heard.

Hadja Lahbib opened the first EU–Mediterranean Peace and Security Forum in Brussels on Wednesday. It fell to the commissioner for equality as the planned keynote speaker, Kaja Kallas, head of the European External Action Service (EEAS) and EU security and foreign policy chief, was conspicuously missing.

The High Representative did not attend Wednesday’s scheduled appearance at the Schuman Security and Defence Forum, either. Her press office told EU Perspectives that Ms Kallas was down with flu. Whether it is a case of ‘political influenza’, an explanation that sprang to mind following major setbacks for Ms Kallas in recent weeks, was not clear at the time of writing.

Ms Lahbib opened the forum with a story from the 12th century. She described Al Idrisi, a cartographer commissioned by King Roger II of Sicily to survey the known world. The result, the Book of Roger, held detailed accounts of countries, cities, rivers, mountains, trade routes, and peoples.
snippet: Security arrangements between the EU and its regional southern partners must address everybody’s concerns, the EU-MED Security Forum 2026 heard.

title: EU strikes overnight deal for faster solar, grid, and charging permits
content:
Homes and businesses installing solar panels, batteries, or charging points could get permits within months. The smallest might need none at all. An EU deal also eases grid applications and makes larger renewable projects share benefits with locals.

Under the deal EU governments and Parliament reached early on Wednesday, permits for solar equipment and batteries installed alongside it would take no more than three months. Stand-alone storage and charging stations would have a six-month deadline. The agreed rules also set a three-month limit for grid connections, extendable to six months where justified.

“We need grid infrastructure for clean, affordable, and homegrown energy and to break our dependence on imported fossil fuels,” said Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment, whose country holds the rotating Council presidency. He spoke after the provisional agreement. Electricity transmission projects currently take around ten years to complete, with permitting accounting for more than half that time.

title: Extreme weather cost EU €270bn in five years. And 2026 is not over
content:
Floods, storms, and droughts have cost the EU more in the past five years than in any other five-year stretch since 1980. Most of that bill never reaches an insurer. Households, businesses, and governments pay it themselves, while Europe’s efforts to adapt fail to keep pace.

Extreme weather events caused approximately €920bn in direct economic losses across EU member states between 1980 and 2025, the European Environment Agency (EEA) reports in its updated data. More than €270bn came in the last five years alone, nearly a third of the total.

The figures make 2021–2025 the costliest five-year period on record, highlighting the growing economic burden of extreme weather across Europe. The estimates cover only direct economic damage, excluding indirect costs such as lost productivity, impacts on GDP, environmental impacts, and consequences for human health.

With extreme weather events expected to intensify further, the agency warns that Europe’s adaptation efforts are not keeping pace. The European Climate Risk Assessment estimates annual losses of at least €175bn across the EU and the UK at 3°C of global warming.

title: EU funding is too slow for modern warfare, says Ukrainian defence tech boss
content:
“If China were to decide to restrict its exports, Ukraine as well as the rest of Europe and the US would feel that immediately,” says Igor Nakonechnyi. The CEO of Project Foundation, a Ukrainian bid to build chip capacity in Europe, tells EU Perspectives why the drone industry depends on China and what Europe can learn from Ukraine’s frontline.

The war in Ukraine has exposed how heavily the world’s drone industry relies on China for critical components. The Fourth Law is a Ukrainian defence technology company that develops autonomous drones for use on the battlefield.

Together with its sister company Odd Systems, which supplies drone cameras, it is working to establish semiconductor manufacturing capacity in Europe through an initiative called Project Foundation. The two firms want to reduce reliance on Chinese suppliers and address a vulnerability that affects Ukraine’s drone industry and Europe’s wider security.

title: Ukraine’s drone war never belonged to Fedorov, says defence entrepreneur
content:
Most wounded soldiers on Ukraine’s front lines are now hit by drones. Fedir Serdiuk, co-founder of defence company MOWA, tells EU Perspectives that Ukraine is ready to join Europe’s defence market. What it lacks are practical ways in.

EU Perspectives first spoke to Mr Serdiuk in April about what the EU can learn from Ukraine’s battlefields. Much has changed since. In July, President Volodymyr Zelensky dismissed Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, and in August Ukraine’s parliament appointed Yevhen Khmara in his place.

We spoke again shortly before the Abu Dhabi peace talks of 10–11 November. For Brussels, his message is clear. “Ukraine is absolutely ready to be integrated with EU defence market and defence space but now it’s a U-turn to find practical and measurable tracks to integrate both industrial-wise.”

It’s been four and a half years since the large-scale invasion by Russia started, and it’s for me every day is a gift. Because it’s the formidable power and very serious military power that Russia presents. Also very brutal and capable, unfortunately, with a lot of resources. So being able to defend as good as we are doing this is itself a very good, a very good scenario.
snippet: Most wounded soldiers on Ukraine’s front lines are now hit by drones. Fedir Serdiuk, co-founder of defence company MOWA, tells EU Perspectives that Ukraine is ready to join Europe’s defence market.

title: ‘Promise without money protects noone.’ Climate-hit health systems get a third of what they need
content:
A new global alliance launched at COP31 will bring together climate and health research funders, as countries face pressure to turn promises into action.

Forty-eight developing countries say they need $3.3bn (approx. €3.0bn) a year to prepare their health systems for climate change. In 2024, international finance covered less than 34 per cent of those needs, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. At the UN climate summit in Antalya (COP31), the EU’s new health pledge is aimed at research.

On 13 November, the European Commission launched the Multilateral Initiative on Climate & Health Research Funding with the Wellcome Trust and public research funders from five continents. The Commission calls it the first global alliance of funders dedicated to climate and health research.

The pressure in Antalya is to deliver, not to promise. “COP31 must be the COP of implementation,” says Brazil’s Health Minister Alexandre Padilha, whose country hosted last year’s summit. “More than making political commitments, we need to turn them into concrete actions.”
snippet: A new global alliance launched at COP31 will bring together climate and health research funders, as countries face pressure to turn promises into action.
creator: Nicole Verbeeck

title: ‘Europe cannot compete at yesterday’s speed’: Pharma industry wants reform, patients demand a say
content:
From clinical trials moving to China to growing concerns over medicine supply chains, Europe’s pharmaceutical sector is facing mounting pressure to become more competitive. The EU’s proposed Biotech Act aims to reverse the trend. But industry and patient groups disagree on the price of making Europe an innovation hub.

The proposed European Biotech Act is intended to strengthen Europe’s position in global pharmaceutical research and development, support innovation, and encourage companies to keep their investments in the EU. Yet a roundtable in the European Parliament revealed differing views on how far the EU should go to attract industry investment and who should benefit from the resulting incentives.

title: We need ‘Friends of Global Europe’: Foreign policy expert on EU’s budget blind spot
content:
When EU governments sit down to negotiate the budget, farm and regional funding have plenty of defenders. Money for the bloc’s work around the world is easier to cut, says development policy expert Alexei Jones. He argues that the EU wants greater influence on the world stage but is unwilling to put money behind that ambition.

The Irish presidency’s latest proposal would cut the Global Europe heading by €33.064 billion, or 17.4 per cent, compared with the European Commission’s original proposal for the 2028–2034 budget (MFF). The instrument funds both development cooperation and projects that advance the EU’s strategic interests.

While cuts to agriculture and cohesion funding spark widespread political controversy, reducing the spending on external action remains relatively undisputed. That is not only remarkable, but also inconsistent with the EU’s wider calls for strategic autonomy and sustainable partnerships, argues Dr Alexei Jones of the European Centre for Development Policy Management (ECDPM). He tells EU Perspectives why the EU needs to rethink the role of its external budget in achieving those goals.
